title: Sarde in Saor
subtitle: Venetian sweet-and-sour marinated sardines with onions, raisins, and pine nuts
excerpt: Sarde in saor is the most ancient of Venetian dishes: fried fresh sardines marinated in sweet-and-sour onions with raisins, pine nuts, and white wine vinegar. The dish must be made at least a day ahead -- the sardines improve as they sit in the marinade. It is Venetian food at its most distinctive.
sourceNotes: Sarde in saor is one of the oldest recorded Venetian dishes, appearing in documents from the fourteenth century. The sweet-and-sour technique (saor means flavour or sauce in Venetian dialect) reflects both the preservation needs of a seafaring city and the Arabic influence on medieval Venetian cooking, which used sugar, vinegar, raisins, and pine nuts together.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be made at least 24 hours ahead. Improves over 48 hours. Will keep for up to 5 days in the fridge.

content.text: Sarde in saor requires patience: the dish must rest in the fridge for at least 24 hours before eating, and is better after 48 hours. The sardines are fried first, then layered with the sweet-and-sour onion mixture. Do not skip the resting time -- the dish is not ready to eat on the day it is made.

items.prepNote: soaked in warm water for 10 minutes then drained

content.text: Dust {{sardines-fresh}} sardines in {{plain-flour}} flour, shaking off the excess. Heat {{vegetable-oil}} oil to 180C in a deep pan and fry the sardines in batches for 2 to 3 minutes until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper. Season with {{salt-table}} salt.

Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil in a large pan over low heat. Cook {{onion}} onion slices very gently for 20 minutes until soft and sweet, not coloured. Add {{white-wine-dry}} wine and {{white-wine-vinegar}} vinegar. Simmer for 5 minutes. Add {{raisins}} raisins and {{pine-nuts}} pine nuts. Season with a little {{salt-table}} salt.
Layer the fried sardines and the onion mixture alternately in a dish, starting and ending with onion. Cover and refrigerate for at least 24 hours. Serve at room temperature.

items.symptom: The sardines have become very soft after marinating
items.cause: This is correct -- the acid in the vinegar 'cooks' the sardines further over 24 hours.
items.fix: Sarde in saor sardines are meant to be soft and almost melting. They are not a crispy dish. If they are too soft for your preference, reduce the resting time to 12 hours.

content.text: Sarde in saor is one of the oldest dishes in Venice, documented since at least the fourteenth century. The sweet-and-sour technique -- vinegar, raisins, and pine nuts -- reflects Arabic cooking that reached Venice through eastern trade. The dish was first made to preserve fried fish for long sea voyages. It is now one of the most common dishes at the small Venetian wine bars (bacari) that line the canals and alleys of the city.
